name: Fireweed
partUsed: Leaves for Poor Louis Farms tea
season: Young leaves are generally gathered before flowering; exact farm timing follows the plants and weather.
habitat: A widespread Alaska perennial often found in open and disturbed ground, including burns, clearings, roadsides, riverbars, and recently deglaciated areas.
aromaFlavor: Leaf tea can be mild, smooth, lightly sweet, and earthy. Fermentation and aging can deepen it toward maltier notes.
culinaryUses: Young shoots and leaves also have documented culinary uses outside this product context
householdUses: The flowers are familiar in Alaska gardens and pollinator habitat, but they are not what makes the farm's fireweed tea
traditionalContext: Fireweed has a long record of food use in Alaska and northern regions. This guide presents that as cultural and historical context, not a treatment claim.
farmUse: Poor Louis Farms makes both loose-leaf fireweed tea and an aged fermented Fireweed Pu'er from the leaves. The bright flowers are part of the plant's identity, not the tea ingredient.
safety: Positive identification matters. Use a trusted local guide or experienced teacher before gathering any wild plant. Follow land rules, harvest lightly, and use the current product label for brewing guidance.

name: Spruce tips
season: A brief spring-to-early-summer window while new growth is still soft; timing varies by place and year.
habitat: Spruce species grow widely in Alaska, but the exact species used in the current sauce is not identified in the public listing.
aromaFlavor: Bright, resinous, citrus-like, and evergreen; intensity shifts quickly as the tip matures.
culinaryUses: Flavor counterpoint in sauces, syrups, salts, and infusions
householdUses: Fresh tips can be used as a visual seasonal reference in field notes and craft work; food and craft material should be kept distinct
traditionalContext: Spruce has many food, material, and cultural uses across northern communities. Those traditions are place- and people-specific and are not claimed here as Poor Louis Farms' heritage.
farmUse: Young spruce tips supply the bright evergreen note in Spruce Tip Hot Sauce.
safety: Never identify conifers by an app alone. Some evergreen plants are toxic, and harvest rules depend on land ownership. Take only positively identified material from places where gathering is allowed.

name: Rosehips
season: Usually late summer into autumn; Alaska species, exposure, and weather change the timing.
habitat: Wild and cultivated roses occur across Alaska. The current pepper-flake listing does not confirm which rose species supplies the hips.
aromaFlavor: Tart, fruity, lightly floral, and a little earthy when dried.
culinaryUses: A tart element in dried seasoning
Commonly explored in syrups, spreads, teas, and baked goods when properly prepared
householdUses: Dried hips can be used in non-food botanical displays when kept clean and clearly labeled
traditionalContext: Rosehips appear in many northern food traditions. This entry stays general because species, community, and preparation traditions differ.
farmUse: Poor Louis Farms combines rosehips with fermented pepper flakes for a tart-and-hot seasoning.
safety: Identify the plant confidently, avoid sprayed roadsides, and remove or strain irritating interior hairs when a preparation calls for it. Follow a tested recipe for preservation.

name: Raspberry leaf
season: Leaf quality changes across the growing season; the farm's exact harvest window is not publicly documented.
habitat: Raspberries may be cultivated or gathered, depending on species and place. The current product listing does not state the species or source plot.
aromaFlavor: Mild, leafy, herbaceous, and softly sweet when infused.
traditionalContext: Raspberry leaf has a broad history in herbal practice. This page makes no pregnancy, reproductive, or medical recommendation.
farmUse: Poor Louis Farms dries raspberry leaves and portions them into tea bags.
safety: Herbal products can be inappropriate for some people or interact with care plans. Ask a qualified clinician about personal concerns, especially during pregnancy, and follow the current label.

name: Calendula
partUsed: Flower heads in the current salve description
season: Cultivated flowering season; harvest timing follows bloom quality rather than a fixed calendar.
habitat: A cultivated garden annual in Alaska. The exact species or cultivar grown at the farm is not publicly confirmed.
aromaFlavor: Warm, green, and lightly resinous; this site does not describe it as a food ingredient in a current product.
culinaryUses: Some calendula species and cultivars have documented culinary uses, but identification and growing conditions matter
traditionalContext: Calendula has a long history in household herbal preparations. Historical use is not evidence that a product treats a condition.
farmUse: The calendula in Poor Louis Farms salve is described as grown at the farm, harvested, and infused into oil before beeswax is added.
safety: For external use as directed by the current product label. Check the full ingredient list before use and stop if irritation occurs. People sensitive to daisy-family plants may wish to use extra care.

name: Árbol chile
season: Cultivated harvest timing depends on heat, maturity, and the growing setup; source and schedule are not published.
habitat: A cultivated chile type. The Square listing confirms the ingredient but does not claim it is farm-grown or Alaska-grown.
aromaFlavor: Clean, direct heat with red-fruit and lightly smoky notes; fermentation adds acidity and savory depth.
traditionalContext: Chiles have deep and diverse culinary histories in the Americas. Poor Louis Farms' use is a contemporary Alaska-made flavor experiment, not a claim to originate those traditions.
farmUse: Árbol chiles are fermented for Spruce Tip Hot Sauce.
safety: Chile oils can irritate skin, eyes, and airways. Handle concentrated chile material carefully and wash tools and hands thoroughly.

name: Whittier sea salt
season: Not presented as a farm-season botanical.
habitat: The current hot-sauce listing identifies Whittier, Alaska, as the salt's place reference. Supplier and harvesting details are not published.
aromaFlavor: Clean salinity that sharpens chile, fermentation, and spruce-tip aromatics.
culinaryUses: Seasoning and flavor balance in Spruce Tip Hot Sauce
traditionalContext: Salt is essential to many fermentation systems, but this guide does not publish a recipe or process ratio.
farmUse: The Square description names Whittier sea salt as one of three defining ingredients in Spruce Tip Hot Sauce.
safety: Do not use this overview as a fermentation formula. Safe fermentation depends on tested ratios, clean equipment, time, temperature, acidity, and product-specific controls.

name: Fermented chile peppers
season: Cultivated harvest timing varies; the pepper variety in Rosehip Pepper Flakes is not publicly named.
habitat: Cultivated. No claim is made that the peppers in the current blend are grown at Poor Louis Farms.
aromaFlavor: Heat and fruit character concentrated by drying, with tang and savory depth from fermentation.
traditionalContext: Fermenting and drying chiles are broad culinary practices with many distinct traditions. The farm's blend is one small-batch interpretation.
farmUse: Fermented pepper flakes provide heat and depth in Rosehip Pepper Flakes.
safety: Handle hot peppers carefully. This overview is not a home-fermentation or preservation recipe; use a tested process from a food-safety authority.
